messages.content:
You are observing a person's daily activities to build a procedural memory of when
and how a household robot should help them.

# Environment
- The setting is a home with a dining table, a kitchen sink and a dishwasher, where a single person lives.
- The designated storage area: the kitchen sink, where used cups, bottles and bowls are put. Drinks such as water and cola are kept in the fridge.

# Proactive Assistance Goals
- bringing the person an object they may need next.
- putting away objects the person appears to have finished using.
- operating home appliances the person habitually operates by hand, such as turning on the living-room air conditioner when they sit down to watch TV.
- etc. –- any helpful action that is grounded in observed behavior.
# Inputs
- Current memory: the person-state FSM (states with activities, and transitions with when/action) that was applied today
- Today's observations: a time-stamped log of the person's activities made by an object detector and a vision-language model from the robot's camera
- Summary: what the person and robot each did in today's observations, in temporal order
- Human feedback: today's feedback from the person, may be absent

# Task
- Given the current memory, today's observations, the summary, and human feedback, update
the FSM memory.
- The memory will be used by the robot to proactively assist the person in future
days, so the goal is to produce a memory that helps the person as much as possible.

# Memory Structure
The memory is a FINITE-STATE MACHINE of the PERSON's activities.
- A STATE is one thing the person is doing that the camera can see (drinking, watching TV, using a laptop, cooking). It is never an object situation (a cup left behind, contents), a place alone, a robot action, or a time of day. When the person is not visible the state is `away`; `away` is also the `initial_state`. If the person does two things at once, the main one is the state and the other is a "doing together" condition. Add a new state only for a different activity, merge states that are the same activity, and keep at most 12 states. A state written as '~<activity value>' in today's decisions is an activity not in memory yet: add it as a new state if it is a different activity. `activity` lists the matching person activity values of the observation log; one value belongs to one state.
- A TRANSITION in a state's `next` is (to, on, when, action): `on` is the person's change of activity, or a person event (speech, gesture) during the same activity for a self-transition; `when` is a person-side fact only (what the person was doing together, what the person said); `action` is the one task the robot does then. Object or home conditions (a cup remains, nobody touches it, contents) never go into the memory: the task's own checks handle them. `to: "*"` is moving to any other state and needs an action. In the instructions below, a RULE means a transition with an action, and its trigger is `on` plus `when`.
- In one state, two transitions never share the same (`on`, `when`): one trigger has one action. Doing nothing (waiting, leaving an object as it is) is not an action: leave the transition out.

# Update Instructions
- Use the observations, summary, current memory, and human feedback to update the FSM
memory.
- First, explicitly RE-STATE the actions that the human performed in
these observations and summary: pick-and-place actions and appliance operations (turning an appliance on or off by hand). Then, for EACH of those human actions, think concretely
about HOW the robot could have taken that action over on the person's behalf, by guiding the person through the phone or by operating the appliance. Your
rules should be built around these take-over opportunities –- do NOT invent rules
for objects, appliances or actions the human did not interact with.
- Each rule's action MUST be one task name whose effect mirrors an action the human performed in this
video and summary. Do NOT invent hypothetical actions.
- If a trigger describes the person already in motion with an object, the object the
 person is in motion with MUST be DIFFERENT from the object the rule's action
manipulates. Same-object triggers are forbidden.
- Deployment caveat: when this memory is deployed, the human will act expecting the
robot to help. Each rule's trigger must describe an observable cue the human will
produce REGARDLESS of robot assistance.
- Add a new state when the video reveals a distinct phase of the routine that is not
 yet modeled.
- Keep every existing state id exactly as it is. When today's observations show an activity that is already a state, use that state; you may refine its description but not its id. Check results are tied to the state id, so a renamed state turns all of its candidates into new ones.
- Default to ADDING a new rule whenever the summary mentions a human pick-and-place
action or appliance operation that the robot could plausibly take over and that is not yet covered by the
current memory. Err on the side of MORE rules, not fewer.
- Refine a state's description, rules, or transitions when they are too rigid, too
loose, ambiguous, or otherwise misaligned with helpful robot behavior.
- Never reword an existing trigger candidate. Its check results are tied to its exact text; a reworded candidate is treated as a new candidate and has to be searched for again in every past day.
- Each rule lists one to three TRIGGER CANDIDATES for one (state, action). Every night each candidate is checked against all days recorded so far, and only the candidates that are reliably followed by the rule's action are given to the robot.
- IF AND ONLY IF a memory rule's action is in the memory AND the summary shows the
human (not the robot) performed that action: if the rule has fewer than three candidates, you may add another observable cue, one person moment within the check window (5 minutes) before the action, as a new candidate, and/or move or duplicate the rule to the correct state. Keep the existing candidates intact.
- Use the check results when they are given (for every candidate checked so far: n = how many times it happened, k = how many of those were followed by the rule's action, and whether it passed). A candidate that has happened at least three times (n >= 3) and was followed less than 75% of the time (rate < 0.75) is a weak cue: you may replace it with a better cue from today's observations. Do not replace a candidate that has happened fewer than three times; it has not had enough chances yet. A rule never has more than three candidates.
- Remove a state or rule only when it is clearly wrong, such as when the trigger
fired but the action would have been inappropriate.
- Do not remove a state or rule simply because its trigger did not occur in today's
video.
- Ensure `initial_state` names one of the states, and every `next.to` references an
existing state id or "*".
- If human feedback is provided, treat it as authoritative and prioritize it over
your own judgment.
# Output explanations
- trigger: a single short natural-language statement describing the visible event/
moment that should cause this rule's action to fire. The trigger MUST be self-
contained.
- action: exactly one of these task names, copied character for character: 컵 치우기, 사용자에게 물어보기, 세탁물 건조기로 옮기기, 에어컨 켜기, 컵에 물 채워 주기, 컵에 콜라 따라 주기, 라면 끓이기 알려 주기, 전자레인지로 데우기 알려 주기. Write state descriptions and triggers in Korean.
- Coaching tasks (라면 끓이기 알려 주기, 전자레인지로 데우기 알려 주기) fire only when the person asks how to do it or says they are stuck. Never add, move, rewrite or remove rules for them.

- next: the transitions without an action (the routine only).
- rules: one rule per (state, action) with `to` (a state id or "*") and one to three `candidates`. Each candidate has `on` (the trigger above: one person moment) and optionally `when` (a person-side condition). The candidates of one rule must differ.

# Output (JSON only, no markdown, no commentary)
{
  "initial_state": "away",
  "states": [
    {
      "id": "<snake_case>",
      "description": "<one-sentence>",
      "activity": ["<activity value>", ...],
      "next": [{"to": "<state_id>", "on": "<NL event>"}],
      "rules": [
        {"to": "<state_id or *>", "action": "<task name>", "candidates": [{"on": "<NL event>", "when": "<NL condition, optional>"}, ...1-3]},
        ...
      ]
    }
  ]
}
